portfolio_return(stock_pct, stock_return, bond_return)


A weighted average of the two returns. Also accepts polars expressions, so it works inside with_columns(). From the Asset Allocation chapter.

Share of the portfolio in stocks, as a decimal.

Yearly stock return, as a decimal.

Yearly bond return, as a decimal.

 float, numpy.ndarray, or polars.Expr

Portfolio returns, as decimals. A polars expression when any input is one.

 TypeError

If an argument is not numeric (or a polars expression).

 ValueError

If an argument contains missing values.

>>> import polars as pl
>>> from perfinpy import portfolio_return

...     bad=portfolio_return(pl.col("stocks"), -0.40, 0.0)

Installation

title: perfinpy
text:
Example
The functions keep the book’s names, arguments, and defaults, so code from a chapter runs unchanged:
from perfinpy import future_value, mortgage_payment, percent_of_income

# rent of $1,500 on a $5,000 monthly income
percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=5000)
#> 30.0

# $10,000 at 7% over four horizons
future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=[5, 10, 20, 30])
#> array([14025.517307  , 19671.5135729 , 38696.84462486, 76122.55042662])

# a $480,000 mortgage at 6% over 30 years
mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30)
#> 2877.842520733233
Rates go in as decimals (0.07 is 7%), ratio functions return percents (30 is 30%), and most functions accept arrays so you can compare options in one call. The user guide has one page for each chapter of the book.

title: Retirement Accounts
text: A retirement account is a container for your investments, and the container decides how they get taxed. Two questions decide most of the value. How much free money does the employer match add? And does paying tax now (Roth) or later (Traditional) leave you with more? In this page I’ll answer both with employer_match() and after_tax_value(), using the numbers from the Retirement Accounts chapter of the book.

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
What if you contribute less?
Many employers enroll new hires at 3%. At that rate the match slice shrinks with your contribution:

match_3 = employer_match(
    salary=45000, contribution_pct=0.03, match_limit_pct=0.06, match_rate=0.50
)
match_3

675.0


At 3% the employer adds only $675, so the default rate leaves $675 a year on the table.

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
Which tax rate wins?
after_tax_value() takes several tax rates at once. Use your rate today for the Roth and your expected rate in retirement for the Traditional account:

tax_rates = [0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24]
pl.DataFrame({
    "tax_rate": tax_rates,
    "after_tax": after_tax_value(
        contribution=1000, tax_rate=tax_rates, rate=0.07, years=40
    ),
})


shape: (4, 2)tax_rateafter_taxf64f640.113477.0120550.1213177.5228990.2211680.0771150.2411380.587958


Find your rate now and your rate later in the table. Whichever account is taxed at the lower rate leaves you more.






WarningLimits



These functions cover the math in the chapter, not every plan rule:

employer_match() handles a single tier match (“50% of the first 6%”). Tiered formulas such as “100% of the first 3%, then 50% of the next 2%” need one call per tier, added together.
employer_match() ignores vesting, the yearly contribution limit ($24,500 in 2026), and any match paid only at year end.
after_tax_value() applies one tax rate to the whole amount. It ignores the 10% early withdrawal penalty, state taxes, and the fact that income in retirement spans several brackets.
after_tax_value() assumes the same return every year and the same investments in both accounts.

title: Asset Allocation
text: Your asset allocation is how you split your investments between stocks and bonds. It does more to decide how your money grows (and how bumpy the ride feels) than which funds you pick. Asset allocation math answers two questions. What does a split do in a good year and a bad year? And how much do you move when you rebalance? In this page I’ll answer both with portfolio_return() and rebalance_amount(), using the numbers from the Asset Allocation chapter of the book.

title: Asset Allocation
text:
Rebalancing every fund at once
rebalance_amount() takes arrays, so one call rebalances every fund in a portfolio. Suppose the chapter’s three fund portfolio (60% US stocks, 30% international stocks, 10% bonds) has drifted to $6,600, $2,500, and $900:

current = [6600, 2500, 900]
pl.DataFrame({
    "fund": ["US stocks", "international stocks", "bonds"],
    "target_pct": [0.60, 0.30, 0.10],
    "current": current,
    "move": rebalance_amount(
        target_pct=[0.60, 0.30, 0.10], total=sum(current), current_amount=current
    ),
})


shape: (3, 4)fundtarget_pctcurrentmovestrf64i64f64"US stocks"0.66600-600.0"international stocks"0.32500500.0"bonds"0.1900100.0


Sell $600 of US stocks and use it to buy the other two. The moves add up to zero, because rebalancing only shifts money between funds.






WarningLimits



Both functions are simple on purpose:

portfolio_return() covers two assets (stocks and bonds) for one year. The returns you pass are assumptions, and it ignores fees, taxes, and inflation.
rebalance_amount() doesn’t check that your targets add up to 100%, and total has to include current_amount.
rebalance_amount() ignores trading costs and the taxes that selling can trigger in a taxable account. Inside a 401(k) or IRA, selling doesn’t trigger taxes.

title: Tracking Spending
text: A bank export tells you every dollar that left your account, but it doesn’t tell you where your money went. To answer that, each transaction needs a category, and the small recurring charges need a second look. The Tracking Spending chapter of the book covers both questions. In this page I’ll answer them with two perfinpy functions. apply_rules() sorts transactions into buckets. subscription_opportunity_cost() shows what a subscription would have grown to if you had invested the money instead.

title: Tracking Spending
text:
When a transaction doesn’t match
New merchants show up every month. The book’s rule is “when in doubt, Other.” A transaction that matches no pattern lands in "Other" until you’ve seen it often enough to deserve its own rule. The code below runs two new transactions through the same rules:

new_transactions = pl.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["Venmo Payment", "SPOTIFY FAMILY PLAN"],
})
apply_rules(df=new_transactions, rules=rules)


shape: (2, 2)DescriptionCategorystrstr"Venmo Payment""Other""SPOTIFY FAMILY PLAN""Subscriptions"


The Venmo payment falls through to "Other". The Spotify charge still lands in "Subscriptions" because apply_rules() ignores case, so "Spotify" matches "SPOTIFY".

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
Where should your savings live, and what does that choice earn? The High-Yield Savings Accounts chapter of the book makes the case for a high yield savings account (HYSA) at an online bank: it’s insured, you can reach the money in a day or two, and it pays far more than a big bank’s basic savings account. In this page I’ll put numbers on that case with hysa_balance(), using the chapter’s $9,600 emergency fund so you can check every result against the book.

The high yield accounts function
hysa_balance() follows the conventions on the Get started page: the APY goes in as a decimal, and every argument accepts arrays.








Function
Returns
Units




hysa_balance()
the balance after growing at an APY for some years
dollars (annual_apy is a decimal; years defaults to 1)





How much does an emergency fund earn in a year?
The chapter follows the $9,600 emergency fund from Emergency Fund into a HYSA paying 4% APY. The APY (annual percentage yield) already includes daily compounding, so a year of growth is one multiplication by 1.04:

one_year = hysa_balance(principal=9600, annual_apy=0.04)
one_year, one_year - 9600

(9984.0, 384.0)


After one year the fund holds $9,984, and $384 of that is interest. years defaults to 1, so the call above doesn’t need it.


How does the balance grow year by year?
Leave the money alone and each year multiplies the previous balance by 1.04 again. The chapter draws each year as a bar split into the money you put in and the interest it has earned so far:



$9,600 at 4% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year


The bluish green base never changes; only the blue interest layer grows. Passing several values to years reproduces every bar in one call:

years = list(range(6))
balances = hysa_balance(principal=9600, annual_apy=0.04, years=years)
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "deposit": [9600] * 6,
    "interest": balances - 9600,
    "balance": balances,
}).with_columns(pl.col("interest", "balance").round(2))


shape: (6, 4)yearsdepositinterestbalancei64i64f64f64096000.09600.019600384.09984.029600783.3610383.36396001198.6910798.69496001630.6411230.64596002079.8711679.87


After five years the fund holds $11,679.87, which is the chapter’s $11,680. That’s $2,080 of growth without putting a dollar of the deposit at risk.


Variations
The chapter compares account types rather than banks. In late 2026 the national average savings rate was 0.39%, a big bank’s basic account often paid 0.01%, and the best online accounts paid 3.8% to 4.2%. annual_apy accepts an array, so one call compares a $10,000 balance across all of them:

apys = [0.0001, 0.0039, 0.038, 0.04, 0.042]
pl.DataFrame({
    "account": ["big bank basic", "national average", "online low", "online typical", "online high"],
    "apy": apys,
    "interest_year_1": hysa_balance(principal=10000, annual_apy=apys) - 10000,
}).with_columns(pl.col("interest_year_1").round(2))


shape: (5, 3)accountapyinterest_year_1strf64f64"big bank basic"0.00011.0"national average"0.003939.0"online low"0.038380.0"online typical"0.04400.0"online high"0.042420.0


The gap between online banks is small: $40 a year separates the low and high ends on $10,000. The gap between an online bank and a big bank’s basic account is large: $400 against $1. As the chapter puts it, pick an online HYSA and don’t overthink which one.






WarningLimits



hysa_balance() grows one lump sum at one rate, so it leaves out a few things:

It assumes the APY never changes. Real HYSA rates move with interest rates, sometimes several times a year.
It doesn’t add deposits along the way. For a fixed monthly deposit, use future_value_series() from Investing Basics.
It ignores taxes on interest and inflation.
It doesn’t know about the $250,000 FDIC limit per account holder per bank. Balances above that need a second bank.
It checks that inputs are numbers, not that they make sense. A negative annual_apy or years returns a result instead of an error.





Putting it together
The chapter’s two headline numbers are an APY and an emergency fund, and both come from other chapters’ functions. Banks sometimes advertise an APR, the rate before compounding. apr_to_apy() from Managing Debt converts it with daily compounding, the way most HYSAs pay:

apy = apr_to_apy(apr=0.0392)
apy

0.03997626956226452


A 3.92% APR compounded daily is an APY of 4.00%. Next, emergency_fund_target() from Emergency Fund sets the balance to park: four months of $2,400 in essential expenses. We can then compare that fund after five years in the HYSA and in a big bank’s basic account:

ef_target = emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=2400, months=4)
in_hysa = hysa_balance(principal=ef_target, annual_apy=apy, years=5)
in_basic = hysa_balance(principal=ef_target, annual_apy=0.0001, years=5)
ef_target, round(in_hysa, 2), round(in_basic, 2)

(9600.0, 11678.54, 9604.8)


The same $9,600 fund grows to $11,678.54 in the HYSA and $9,604.80 at the big bank, a difference of $2,074. Finally, ef_growth() from the Emergency Fund chapter does the same math in months, which helps when a goal doesn’t land on a whole year:

ef_growth(balance=ef_target, apy=0.04, months=[12, 18])

array([ 9984.        , 10181.72216474])


Twelve months matches hysa_balance() with the default one year, and 18 months shows the balance halfway through year two.


Recap
A HYSA keeps your savings safe and reachable while paying hundreds of times what a basic account pays. hysa_balance() grows a balance at an APY, and passing several years or several APYs compares horizons and accounts in one call. With apr_to_apy(), emergency_fund_target(), and ef_growth(), it shows what an emergency fund earns while it waits.

High-Yield Savings Accounts in Personal Finance: a field manual

title: Managing Debt
text: Lenders quote whichever number makes a loan look cheapest, and they count on borrowers not running the math. The book’s Managing Debt chapter runs that math. It asks what a balance really costs, how much student debt a salary can carry, which ratios lenders check, and which debt to pay first. In this page I’ll answer the same questions with perfinpy’s 11 managing debt functions. Each example uses the chapter’s numbers, so you can check every result against the book.

title: Managing Debt
text:
APR vs. APY
The chapter’s example is a credit card with a 24% APR that compounds daily, carrying a $5,000 balance. Credit card companies quote the APR, but compounding (charging interest on interest you haven’t paid yet) means the balance grows faster than the APR suggests.
Both bars below represent one year of interest on the same balance. The shorter bar is what the APR implies; the taller bar is what you actually owe:



APR cost vs. APY cost on a $5,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)


The APY (annual percentage yield) is the effective yearly rate once compounding is included. apr_to_apy() converts one to the other, with periods_per_year defaulting to 365 for daily compounding:

apy = apr_to_apy(apr=0.24)
apy

0.27114889144128895


A 24% APR compounded daily is really 27.1% a year. On the $5,000 balance, that gap is about $156 of interest the quoted rate never mentions.

title: Managing Debt
section: How long does a minimum payment take?
text:
How long does a minimum payment take?
The chapter’s next example is a $5,000 balance at 22% APR with a $100 minimum payment. A $100 payment sounds reasonable until you see how little of it reaches the balance. The principal is the amount you borrowed; interest is what the lender charges on top.



Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes


Only the principal slice shrinks the debt. As the balance falls, the interest slice shrinks too, so each payment retires a little more principal than the one before. months_to_payoff() accounts for that, compounding interest monthly at apr / 12:

first_interest = 5000 * 0.22 / 12
card_months = months_to_payoff(balance=5000, monthly_payment=100, apr=0.22)
first_interest, card_months

(91.66666666666667, 136.77905405676316)


The first month’s interest is about $92, so only $8 of the first payment touches the balance. Paying the minimum clears the card in about 137 months (11.4 years), and the payments add up to about $13,678 on a $5,000 balance. Minimum payments are designed to keep you in debt for years.

title: Managing Debt
section: What does the loan term cost?
text:
What does the loan term cost?
An installment loan is one you repay in equal monthly payments, like a car loan or a mortgage. For these loans, total interest is the number that should drive the decision. The chapter’s example is a $20,000 used car loan at 7%. It runs either 6 years at $340.98 a month or 4 years at $478.92 a month.
The amount borrowed is the same either way. The bars below stack the principal and interest layers, so the cost of the longer term is visible:



$20,000 car loan at 7%: principal vs. interest for 6 year and 4 year terms


Subtract the principal from everything you pay and the interest layer is what’s left. total_interest() accepts arrays, so both terms fit in one call:

car_interest = total_interest(
    monthly_payment=[340.98, 478.92],
    n_months=[72, 48],
    principal=20000,
)
car_interest

array([4550.56, 2988.16])


The 6 year loan costs $4,550.56 in interest, and the 4 year loan costs $2,988.16. Shortening the term saves $1,562.40, which is the math behind the 20/4/10 car rule (20% down, no more than 4 years, transportation under 10% of gross income).

title: Managing Debt
text:
The 1x rule
The 1x rule says total student debt at graduation should not exceed your expected first year salary. The chapter’s example borrower has $45,000 in loans and a $42,000 starting salary, repaying on a standard 10 year plan at 6.5%.
Picture what you borrowed and what your first job pays as two bars side by side. The rule says the loan bar shouldn’t run past the salary bar:



$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary


loan_income_ratio() divides the loan bar by the salary bar. monthly_standard_payment() then spreads the loan, plus interest, over 120 equal payments, with the 6.5% rate and 10 year term as defaults:

ratio = loan_income_ratio(loan_total=45000, expected_salary=42000)
student_payment = monthly_standard_payment(principal=45000)
ratio, student_payment

(1.0714285714285714, 510.9658974901199)


The ratio is 1.07, so this borrower is a little over the 1x rule. The standard payment is about $511 a month, or roughly $0.0114 a month for every dollar borrowed. The 1x rule is a ceiling, not a target; lower earning majors often need a lower personal cap.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Income driven repayment
When the 1x rule is out of reach, federal income driven repayment (IDR) plans cap payments as a share of discretionary income. Discretionary income is your AGI (adjusted gross income, from your tax return) minus a protected multiple of the Federal Poverty Guideline. The chapter’s example is a $50,000 AGI under IBR. IBR protects 1.5 times the 2026 guideline ($15,960) and charges 10% on whatever is left.
Think of the AGI as one bar. The plan protects the first part of it, and the payment is a small slice of what’s left:



$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment


idr_monthly_payment() subtracts the protected part, takes the payment rate of what’s left, and divides by 12. The defaults are the IBR terms for loans from July 2014 on; older IBR loans use a 15% rate:

ibr = idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000)
ibr_old = idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000, payment_rate=0.15)
ibr, ibr_old

(217.17, 325.75)


IBR comes to $217.17 a month, and $325.75 for loans made before July 2014. IDR plans change with Congress, the courts, and the Department of Education, so check current terms at studentaid.gov before enrolling.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Debt to income ratio
The chapter pictures a first job paying $45,000 a year, or $3,750 a month in gross income. Its debts are a $511 student loan payment, a $450 car payment, and $100 in credit card minimums. Gross income is your pay before taxes, and the bar below splits it into what goes to debt and what’s left:



$3,750 gross monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income


DTI (debt to income) is just the debt slice as a share of the whole bar. dti_ratio() returns it as a percent:

debt_payments = {"student_loan": 511, "car": 450, "cards": 100}
dti = dti_ratio(
    monthly_debt_payments=sum(debt_payments.values()),
    gross_monthly_income=45000 / 12,
)
dti

28.293333333333333


The $1,061 in monthly debt payments take about 28% of gross income. The chapter calls 20% to 35% manageable but worth watching; above 43%, most mortgage lenders won’t approve you.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Credit utilization
Credit utilization is how much of your available credit you’re using. Credit scores penalize high utilization because using most of your available credit is a sign of money trouble. The chapter’s example is a $900 balance on a first card with a $3,000 limit:



$900 balance against a $3,000 credit limit: used vs. unused


credit_utilization() divides the used slice by the whole limit and returns a percent:

utilization = credit_utilization(balance=900, credit_limit=3000)
utilization

30.0


The card sits at 30% utilization, right at the threshold. Keep utilization under 30% on each card and across all cards; under 10% (a $300 balance on this card) is ideal.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Pay off or invest?
The chapter compares a 5% student loan against an expected 7% stock market return. The math slightly favors investing, but the bar model adds what the math alone misses:



Guaranteed 5% debt payoff vs. expected 7% investment return


payoff_vs_invest() compares the two rates (as decimals) and returns the option that wins on paper:

loan_rate = 0.05
expected_return = 0.07
payoff_vs_invest(loan_rate=loan_rate, expected_return=expected_return)

'Invest the difference'


Investing wins by about 2.0 percentage points a year. But the return from paying off the loan is guaranteed, and the investment return is not. A guaranteed 5% beats a probable 7% for many people psychologically, so run the math, then add your peace of mind premium.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Avalanche vs. snowball
The chapter’s example has three credit cards: Card A ($1,000 at 18%), Card B ($5,000 at 24%), and Card C ($2,000 at 15%). The avalanche method pays the highest APR first; the snowball method pays the smallest balance first. Both attack the same three debts, just in a different order:



Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)


Both functions take a list of debts (one dict per debt) and return a new, sorted list. order_avalanche() needs an apr key, and order_snowball() needs a balance key. Wrapping the result in pl.DataFrame() prints it as a table:

debts = [
    {"name": "Card A", "balance": 1000, "apr": 0.18},
    {"name": "Card B", "balance": 5000, "apr": 0.24},
    {"name": "Card C", "balance": 2000, "apr": 0.15},
]
pl.DataFrame(order_avalanche(debts))


shape: (3, 3)namebalanceaprstri64f64"Card B"50000.24"Card A"10000.18"Card C"20000.15



pl.DataFrame(order_snowball(debts))


shape: (3, 3)namebalanceaprstri64f64"Card A"10000.18"Card C"20000.15"Card B"50000.24


Avalanche wins on paper because a dollar sent to the highest APR stops the most interest. The code below shows how much interest an extra $100 stops next month on each card:

extra_saved = {d["name"]: 100 * d["apr"] / 12 for d in debts}
extra_saved

{'Card A': 1.5, 'Card B': 2.0, 'Card C': 1.25}


An extra $100 on Card B stops $2.00 of interest, compared with $1.50 on Card A. Snowball pays off Card A first, which costs a little more but delivers a win sooner. If that quick win is the price of actually finishing, it’s often worth it; if you’re disciplined enough for avalanche, take the savings.

title: Emergency Fund
text: An emergency fund is cash set aside so a car repair or a job loss doesn’t end up on a credit card. Building one comes down to four questions. How big should the fund be, and how long will it take to fill? How much should you save each month to finish by a deadline, and what does the fund earn in a savings account? In this page I’ll answer them with emergency_fund_target(), months_to_ef_goal(), monthly_contribution_needed(), and ef_growth(). The examples below use the numbers from the Emergency Fund chapter of the book, where each formula is built from scratch.

title: Emergency Fund
text:
Longer deadlines mean smaller payments
The same comparison works in reverse. The code below finds the monthly amount needed to close the $8,400 gap in one, one and a half, or two years:

deadline_months = [12, 18, 24]
deadlines = pl.DataFrame({
    "months": deadline_months,
    "monthly": monthly_contribution_needed(
        target=target,
        current_balance=saved,
        months=deadline_months,
    ),
})
deadlines


shape: (3, 2)monthsmonthlyi64i64127001846724350


Stretching the deadline from one year to two drops the monthly amount from $700 to $350.






WarningLimits




emergency_fund_target() doesn’t choose the number of months for you. The default of 3 is the low end of the range, so pass a larger months for variable income or dependents.
months_to_ef_goal() and monthly_contribution_needed() ignore interest, so they slightly overstate the time and money needed when the fund sits in a HYSA. Both round up and return 0 when the balance already meets the target.
monthly_contribution and months must be greater than 0. A zero raises a ValueError instead of returning inf.
ef_growth() assumes the APY stays fixed and nothing goes in or out during the period. Pass the APY as a decimal (0.04), not a percent (4).

title: Insurance
text: Insurance math helps with two everyday choices. Which deductible should you pick, and which health plan costs less over a year? The Insurance chapter of the book answers both with a little arithmetic. In this page I’ll answer the same questions with break_even_years() and plan_cost(), using the chapter’s numbers so you can check every result against the book.

title: Insurance
section: Health plans across many kinds of year
text:
Health plans across many kinds of year
Most years fall somewhere between healthy and worst. One call per plan covers a range of medical bills:

bills = [0.0, 300.0, 1000.0, 2500.0, 5000.0, float("inf")]
pl.DataFrame({
    "medical_cost": bills,
    "plan_a": plan_cost(monthly_premium=100, medical_cost=bills, oop_max=3000),
    "plan_b": plan_cost(monthly_premium=40, medical_cost=bills, oop_max=5000, employer_hsa=500),
})


shape: (6, 3)medical_costplan_aplan_bf64f64f640.01200.0-20.0300.01500.0280.01000.02200.0980.02500.03700.02480.05000.04200.04980.0inf4200.04980.0


With no medical bills at all, Plan B’s cost is negative: the employer’s $500 is more than the $480 of premiums. Plan B stays cheaper until the bills pass about $4,220. Past that point Plan A has hit its maximum, and it comes out ahead.






WarningLimits



Both functions use the simple version of the math in the chapter. A few limits apply:

plan_cost() assumes you pay every medical bill up to the out of pocket maximum. For plans with coinsurance, it slightly overstates the cost.
plan_cost() ignores copays, tax savings from HSA contributions, and what HSA money could earn if invested.
break_even_years() assumes the premium savings are the same every year and ignores premium increases after a claim.
break_even_years() raises a ValueError when yearly_savings is zero or negative. Text raises a TypeError, and nan raises a ValueError in either function.

title: Financial Goals
text:
A goal without a number and a date is a wish. Once you have both, two questions are left: how much do you set aside each month, and which goal do you fund first when you can’t fund them all? In this page I’ll answer both with monthly_for_goal() and months_to_fund(), using the numbers from the Financial Goals chapter of the book so you can check every result.

The goal functions
Both functions accept arrays and follow the conventions on the Get started page.








Function
Returns
Units




monthly_for_goal()
the monthly deposit that grows into a goal
dollars per month (annual_rate is a decimal)


months_to_fund()
months to save a goal with no interest
whole months, rounded up (an int)





How much should you save each month?
The chapter’s example is a $15,000 down payment in five years. The money sits in a high yield savings account earning 4% a year. Without interest you would divide $15,000 by 60 months and save $250 a month. Interest does part of the work, so you can save a little less.
The bar below is the $15,000 goal. Most of it comes from your deposits, and interest fills in the rest:



A $15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest


monthly_for_goal() works backward from the future value of a series of deposits. It asks which monthly deposit grows into the goal, compounding at annual_rate / 12:

monthly = monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60)
monthly

226.2478308289896


You need about $226.25 a month, which is $23.75 less than saving without interest. Over five years your deposits total $13,575, and interest adds the other $1,425.


Which goal comes first?
Say you can save $600 a month toward two goals: a $3,000 trip and a $9,000 car. You can fund them one at a time (trip first, then car), or split the $600 evenly until the trip is paid for and then send everything to the car.
Each bar below is a goal on a timeline. It starts at month 0 and ends the month the goal is fully funded:



Two goals funded with $600 a month: one at a time vs. split evenly


months_to_fund() divides the goal by the monthly amount going to it and rounds up to a whole month. The last goal is done when all of the money is saved, so its goal is the total of both:

one_at_a_time = (
    months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=600),
    months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=600),
)
split_evenly = (
    months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=300),
    months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=600),
)
one_at_a_time, split_evenly

((5, 20), (10, 20))


The trip finishes at month 5 one at a time, or month 10 split evenly. The car finishes at month 20 either way. The order only decides which goal you get first.


Variations
Passing several rates to annual_rate shows how much interest helps the down payment goal. The 0% row is the plain $15,000 ÷ 60:

rates = [0.0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.05]
pl.DataFrame({
    "annual_rate": rates,
    "monthly": monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=rates, months=60),
})


shape: (4, 2)annual_ratemonthlyf64f640.0250.00.02237.9164010.04226.2478310.05220.568505


Each point of interest trims the deposit by a few dollars a month. Time matters more. The same goal over three, five, and seven years:

months = [36, 60, 84]
pl.DataFrame({
    "months": months,
    "monthly": monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=months),
    "months_no_interest": months_to_fund(goal=15000, monthly=[400, 250, 180]),
})


shape: (3, 3)monthsmonthlymonths_no_interesti64f64i6436392.8597753860226.2478316084155.03209584


The last column runs the other direction: it asks how long $400, $250, or $180 a month takes with no interest at all.






WarningLimits



monthly_for_goal() assumes the same rate every month and a deposit at the end of each month. It ignores taxes on interest and inflation, so a goal priced in today’s dollars will cost more later. months_to_fund() ignores interest entirely and rounds up, so it gives the first month the goal is fully funded.
Both functions stop with a ValueError when the divisor isn’t positive:

months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=0)


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[6], line 1
----> 1 months_to_fund(goal=3000, monthly=0)

File ~/projects/pkgs/Python/perfinpy/src/perfinpy/financial_goals.py:89, in months_to_fund(goal, monthly)
     56 """Whole months to fund a goal with no interest.
     57 
     58 From the [Financial Goals](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/financial_goals.html)
   (...)     86 (5, 20)
     87 """
     88 goal = _as_numeric(goal, "goal")
---> 89 monthly = _as_positive(monthly, "monthly")
     90 return _ceil(goal / monthly)

File ~/projects/pkgs/Python/perfinpy/src/perfinpy/_checks.py:38, in _as_positive(x, arg)
     36 out = _as_numeric(x, arg)
     37 if np.any(np.asarray(out) <= 0):
---> 38     raise ValueError(f"`{arg}` must be greater than 0.")
     39 return out

ValueError: `monthly` must be greater than 0.



monthly_for_goal() does the same when months is 0 or negative.




Putting it together
Back to the $600 a month. Suppose the down payment comes first, and whatever is left goes to the trip and the car. The down payment takes the amount we found above, and months_to_fund() shows how long the remainder needs for both smaller goals:

down_payment = monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60)
left_over = 600 - down_payment
both_goals = months_to_fund(goal=3000 + 9000, monthly=left_over)
round(left_over, 2), both_goals

(373.75, 33)


With $373.75 a month left over, the trip and the car take 33 months instead of 20. That trade is the real decision: the down payment stays on schedule, and the smaller goals wait longer. The Major Purchases page picks up the down payment and asks what the mortgage would cost.


Recap
A goal needs a number, a date, and a monthly amount. monthly_for_goal() turns the number and the date into the monthly amount, with interest doing part of the work. months_to_fund() shows that the order of your goals changes which one you reach first, but not when the last one is done.

Financial Goals in Personal Finance: a field manual

title: Automating Savings
text:
Once you know your savings rate and where the money will live, how much should leave each paycheck automatically? The Automating Savings chapter of the book argues for paying yourself first: savings move out before you see them, so saving no longer depends on willpower. In this page I’ll answer the “how much” question with monthly_savings(), using the chapter’s $4,000 gross monthly pay so you can check every result against the book. Then we’ll borrow functions from other chapters to follow the automated money into an emergency fund and an investment account.

The automating savings function
monthly_savings() follows the conventions on the Get started page. Note the units: its savings_rate argument is a decimal (0.20), while the savings_rate() function from Savings Strategies returns a percent (20.0).








Function
Returns
Units




monthly_savings()
the monthly amount to pay yourself first
dollars per month (savings_rate is a decimal)





How much should you automate each month?
The chapter’s example earns $48,000 a year, or $4,000 a month before taxes, and aims for a 20% savings rate. The rate is measured on gross pay here because 401(k) contributions come out before taxes.
Picture the gross paycheck as one bar cut into five equal fifths. One fifth goes to savings before you ever see it, and the rest is what you live on:



$4,000 of gross monthly pay with 20% automated to savings


Taking one fifth of the bar is the same as multiplying it by 0.20, which is what monthly_savings() does:

automated = monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income=4000, savings_rate=0.20)
automated

800.0


The paycheck sends $800 a month to savings, which leaves $3,200 for taxes and everything else.


How do you split it across accounts?
In practice the 20% goes to several places at once. The chapter splits it into an emergency fund, a 401(k) contribution large enough to get a typical employer match, and sinking funds (money set aside each month for a known future bill). savings_rate accepts an array, so one call prices every destination:

split = pl.DataFrame({
    "destination": ["emergency fund", "401(k) match", "sinking funds"],
    "rate": [0.10, 0.05, 0.05],
})
split = split.with_columns(
    amount=monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income=4000, savings_rate=split["rate"]),
)
split


shape: (3, 3)destinationrateamountstrf64f64"emergency fund"0.1400.0"401(k) match"0.05200.0"sinking funds"0.05200.0


The three amounts add up to $800, the same 20% from the bar model. Payroll takes the 401(k) share before taxes, so the direct deposit split only needs to send the other $600 to the HYSA.


Variations
The chapter’s long game is escalation: raise the savings rate with each raise instead of cutting spending. Its timeline pairs a growing salary with a rate that climbs five points every two years. Dividing each salary by 12 gives the monthly income, and arrays in both arguments price every year at once. future_value_series() from Investing Basics then shows what 30 years of each monthly amount could grow to at 7% (rate is per month here, so the yearly return is divided by 12):

salary = [50000, 54000, 58000, 63000]
rate = [0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30]
monthly = monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income=[s / 12 for s in salary], savings_rate=rate)
pl.DataFrame({
    "year": [1, 3, 5, 7],
    "salary": salary,
    "rate": rate,
    "monthly": monthly.round(2),
    "after_30_years": future_value_series(contribution=monthly, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12).round().astype(int),
})


shape: (4, 5)yearsalaryratemonthlyafter_30_yearsi64i64f64f64i641500000.15625.07624823540000.2900.010979745580000.251208.3314741327630000.31575.01921454


The monthly amounts match the chapter’s $625, $900, $1,208, and $1,575, and the 30 year values match its $762k to $1.92M range. Most of that jump is paid for by raises, not by spending less.






WarningLimits



monthly_savings() is a single multiplication, so it leaves a few things to you:

savings_rate is a decimal. Passing 20 instead of 0.20 returns $80,000, not $800, and no error is raised.
It doesn’t check ranges. A negative income or a rate above 1 returns a result instead of an error.
It uses whatever income you give it. The chapter uses gross pay; a rate measured on take home pay gives a smaller amount.
It assumes a steady paycheck. For gig or commission income, the chapter suggests passing your average monthly income over the last six months.





Putting it together
Back to the $4,000 paycheck. The emergency fund line gets $400 a month until the fund is full. The Emergency Fund chapter’s first job has $2,400 a month in essential expenses, a four month target, and $1,200 already saved. emergency_fund_target() and months_to_ef_goal() show how long the automation takes to finish the job:

ef_monthly = monthly_savings(gross_monthly_income=4000, savings_rate=0.10)
ef_target = emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=2400, months=4)
ef_months = months_to_ef_goal(
    target=ef_target, current_balance=1200, monthly_contribution=ef_monthly
)
ef_target, ef_months

(9600.0, 21)


The $9,600 fund is full in 21 months without a single decision along the way. Once it’s full, the chapter sends the $400 to investing instead. future_value_series() shows what that redirected transfer could become over 30 years at 7%:

redirected = future_value_series(contribution=ef_monthly, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12)
redirected

487988.39831037784


The same $400 transfer could grow to about $487,988. As a last check, percent_of_income() from Budgeting turns the automated dollars back into a rate. It returns a percent, the reverse of the decimal monthly_savings() takes:

percent_of_income(expense=automated, income=4000)

20.0




Recap
Automation makes saving the default instead of a monthly decision. monthly_savings() turns a savings rate into the dollar amount to automate, and its array inputs price a split across accounts or a whole escalation plan in one call. Paired with the emergency fund and investing functions, it shows where those automated dollars end up.

title: Budgeting
text: Most budgeting decisions come down to a handful of small calculations. You need to know how big a slice of your paycheck an expense takes and what a daily habit costs over a year. You also need to know what money spent today could have grown into, and how long an upfront purchase takes to pay for itself. The Budgeting chapter of the book builds each of these from scratch. In this page I’ll answer the same questions with percent_of_income(), to_annual(), to_monthly(), opportunity_cost(), and months_to_break_even(), using the chapter’s numbers so you can check every result against the book.

title: Budgeting
text:
Most budgets work in months
to_monthly() goes in the other direction. It converts a daily, weekly, or annual amount to a monthly one, which is the unit most budgets use. Here is the coffee habit per month:

coffee_month = to_monthly(amount=5, period="daily")
coffee_month

152.20000000000002


Coffee runs $152.20 a month, which matches the monthly bar above. The chapter’s second example converts $150 a week in groceries to a monthly amount:

groceries_month = to_monthly(amount=150, period="weekly")
groceries_month

649.5


Groceries come to $649.50 a month. That is more than four weeks’ worth, because a month holds about 4.33 weeks.

title: Budgeting
section: One call compares every time horizon
text:
One call compares every time horizon
The same approach works for time horizons. Passing several values to years reproduces each checkpoint in the car bar model:

horizons = [0, 5, 10, 20, 30]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": horizons,
    "value": opportunity_cost(amount=25000, rate=0.07, years=horizons),
})


shape: (5, 2)yearsvaluei64f64025000.0535063.7932681049178.7839322096742.11156230190306.376067








WarningLimits



to_monthly() uses rounded factors (30.44 days and 4.33 weeks per month), while to_annual() uses 365 days and 52 weeks per year. A round trip through both functions drifts slightly. The weekly grocery bill gives a different yearly total depending on the path:

(
    to_annual(amount=150, period="weekly"),
    to_annual(amount=groceries_month, period="monthly"),
)

(7800.0, 7794.0)


A few other limits apply:

to_annual() accepts "daily", "weekly", or "monthly", and to_monthly() accepts "daily", "weekly", or "annual". Any other period raises a ValueError.
opportunity_cost() assumes the same return every year and ignores inflation, taxes, and fund fees.
months_to_break_even() assumes the savings are the same every month and ignores what the upfront cost could have earned if invested.
percent_of_income() and months_to_break_even() raise a ValueError when income or monthly_savings is zero or negative.

title: Taxes
text:
Taxes are the biggest bill most people pay, and two questions come up again and again. How much federal income tax do you owe on your salary? And how much of a raise do you keep once a higher bracket takes its share? The Taxes chapter of the book answers both by slicing income into brackets. In this page I’ll answer the same questions with income_tax() and raise_kept(), using the chapter’s numbers so you can check every result against the book.

The tax functions
Both functions take single numbers only (see the conventions table in Get started). To compare several incomes, loop over them; the Variations section shows how.








Function
Returns
Units




income_tax()
2026 federal income tax for a single filer
dollars per year


raise_kept()
the part of a raise left after federal income tax
dollars per year





How much tax do you owe on a salary?
The chapter’s example is a $45,000 salary for a single filer in 2026. The question is the federal income tax bill, and what share of the salary it takes.
Think of the salary as one long bar. The first $16,100 is covered by the standard deduction and isn’t taxed. The next $12,400 is taxed at 10%. The last $16,500 is taxed at 12%:



A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets


income_tax() subtracts the deduction, multiplies each slice by its own rate, and adds up the slices:

tax = income_tax(income=45000)
effective = tax / 45000
tax, effective

(3220.0, 0.07155555555555555)


The tax is $3,220, an effective rate of 7.2%. That is well below 12%, the marginal rate on this salary’s last dollar. The effective rate is a decimal here because we divided it ourselves; income_tax() returns dollars, not a rate.


How much of a raise do you keep?
Now imagine you earn $66,000 and get a $2,000 raise. Taxable income goes from $49,900 to $51,900, which crosses the 22% line at $50,400. The fear is that the higher bracket eats the raise.
The bar below is just the raise. The first $500 fills the rest of the 12% bracket, and only the last $1,500 is taxed at 22%:



A $2,000 raise that crosses into the 22% bracket


raise_kept() takes the tax on the new income, subtracts the tax on the old income, and takes that difference out of the raise:

kept = raise_kept(old_income=66000, raise_amount=2000)
extra_tax = income_tax(income=68000) - income_tax(income=66000)
kept, extra_tax

(1610.0, 390.0)


You keep $1,610 of the $2,000 raise, and the extra tax is $390. Crossing into a higher bracket never makes a raise cost you money; only the dollars above the line pay the higher rate.


The call stack
raise_kept() doesn’t have its own bracket table. It calls income_tax() twice, once on the new income and once on the old income, and subtracts the two results. The tree below shows that relationship:

from rich import print
from rich.tree import Tree

tree = Tree("raise_kept()")
tree.add("income_tax(old_income + raise_amount)")
tree.add("income_tax(old_income)")
print(tree)

raise_kept()
├── income_tax(old_income + raise_amount)
└── income_tax(old_income)
Any change to the brackets in income_tax() flows straight into raise_kept().


Variations
Because both functions take single numbers, a list comprehension compares several salaries. The table below puts the tax and the effective rate side by side:

incomes = [30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000]
taxes = [income_tax(income=i) for i in incomes]
pl.DataFrame({
    "income": incomes,
    "tax": taxes,
    "effective_rate": [t / i for t, i in zip(taxes, incomes)],
})


shape: (5, 3)incometaxeffective_ratei64f64f64300001420.00.047333450003220.00.071556660005740.00.0869710000013170.00.131715000024734.00.164893


The effective rate climbs with income, but it stays below each salary’s top bracket. The same pattern works for raises. Here is a $2,000 raise at each salary:

pl.DataFrame({
    "income": incomes,
    "kept": [raise_kept(old_income=i, raise_amount=2000) for i in incomes],
})


shape: (5, 2)incomekepti64f64300001760.0450001760.0660001610.01000001560.01500001520.0








WarningLimits



income_tax() hard codes the 2026 federal brackets for a single filer and a $16,100 standard deduction. A few other limits apply:

Other years, married filers, and heads of household need different brackets, which the function doesn’t take.
You can pass a different deduction (for example, itemized deductions), but not different brackets.
Neither function counts credits, FICA (7.65%), state or local taxes, or self employment tax.
Both functions take single numbers only. A list or array raises a ValueError; text raises a TypeError.





Putting it together
Back to the $45,000 salary. Federal income tax is only part of what comes out of the paycheck. FICA (Social Security and Medicare) takes 7.65% of every dollar, with no deduction. percent_of_income() from the Budgeting page shows how much of the salary the two together claim:

salary = 45000
fica = salary * 0.0765
federal = income_tax(income=salary)
total = fica + federal
total_share = percent_of_income(expense=total, income=salary)
fica, federal, total_share

(3442.5, 3220.0, 14.805555555555555)


FICA takes $3,442.50 and federal income tax takes $3,220. Together they claim 14.8% of the salary, before any state tax.
Next, a $2,000 raise on the same salary. All of it stays in the 12% bracket, so you keep a little more than in the $66,000 example:

raise_kept(old_income=salary, raise_amount=2000)

1760.0


This number is before FICA, which takes another 7.65% of the raise.


Recap
Tax brackets apply to slices of income, not the whole salary. income_tax() adds up the tax on each slice, and dividing by income gives the effective rate. raise_kept() calls income_tax() twice to show that a raise always leaves you with more money.

Taxes in Personal Finance: a field manual

title: Major Purchases
text: A home is the biggest purchase most people ever make, and small percentages turn into tens of thousands of dollars. The Major Purchases chapter of the book asks three questions: when does renting beat buying, what will the mortgage cost each month, and where does the first payment go? In this page I’ll answer them with rent_buy_threshold(), mortgage_payment(), and first_payment_split(), using the chapter’s numbers so you can check each result against the book.

title: Major Purchases
text:
Call stack
first_payment_split() doesn’t repeat the payment formula. It calls mortgage_payment(), which uses the internal _annuity_factor() helper (the same one behind monthly_for_goal()):

from rich import print
from rich.tree import Tree

tree = Tree("first_payment_split()")
tree.add("mortgage_payment()").add("_annuity_factor()")
print(tree)

first_payment_split()
└── mortgage_payment()
    └── _annuity_factor()

title: Get started
text: perfinpy holds the Python functions from Personal Finance: a field manual. Each chapter of the book builds its calculations from scratch so you can see how the formula works. This package collects those same functions, documents them, and tests them, so you can use them without copying code out of the book. On this page I’ll cover how to install perfinpy and the conventions every function follows. Then we’ll take a short tour with one example from each part of the book.

Foundations
Rent of $1,500 on a $5,000 monthly income:

rent_share = percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=5000)

title: Index Funds
text: You can’t control what the market does, but you can control what you pay. Index fund math is about that one thing: what fees cost you. A fee looks tiny for a single year, and it comes out every year, so each dollar it takes stops growing. In this page I’ll measure both with yearly_fee() and future_value_after_fees(), using the numbers from the Index Funds chapter of the book.

title: Index Funds
text:
Comparing expense ratios
The chapter suggests looking for funds under 0.10%. Passing a range of expense ratios shows what each one leaves after 40 years:

ratios = [0.0003, 0.0004, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01]
pl.DataFrame({
    "expense_ratio": ratios,
    "fee_on_10k": yearly_fee(balance=10000, expense_ratio=ratios),
    "after_40_years": future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, ratios, 40),
})


shape: (5, 3)expense_ratiofee_on_10kafter_40_yearsf64f64f640.00033.0780841.7341920.00044.0778654.7099260.00110.0765675.2372660.00550.0685085.6760240.01100.0597447.220299


The difference between 0.03% and 0.10% is small. The difference between 0.10% and 1% is not.






WarningLimits



A few things these functions leave out:

yearly_fee() uses one balance. A fund charges its fee on your balance through the year, so a growing account pays a little more than this.
future_value_after_fees() subtracts the expense ratio from the return and assumes both stay the same every year. Contributions are monthly, made at the end of each month.
Neither function counts sales charges (loads), trading costs, advisor fees, or taxes in a taxable account.

title: Savings Strategies
text:
How much of your paycheck do you actually keep? The Savings Strategies chapter of the book argues that your savings rate is the one number worth tracking above all others, because it sets how fast wealth builds. In this page I’ll answer that question with savings_rate(), using the chapter’s numbers so you can check every result against the book. Then we’ll borrow a few functions from other chapters to follow one paycheck from savings rate to emergency fund to long term investing.

The savings strategies function
savings_rate() follows the conventions on the Get started page. Like the other ratio functions, it returns a percent, not a decimal.








Function
Returns
Units




savings_rate()
the share of income not spent
percent (15 is 15%); negative when spending exceeds income





What is your savings rate?
The chapter’s first job takes home $3,200 a month and spends $2,720 of it. Every dollar of the paycheck goes to either spending or savings, so the question is how big the savings slice is.
Think of the take home pay as one bar. Spending fills most of it, and savings is the slice left at the end:



$3,200 take home pay: spending and savings


savings_rate() subtracts spending from income, divides by income, and multiplies by 100:

first_job_rate = savings_rate(income=3200, spending=2720)
first_job_rate

15.0


The first job saves 15% of take home pay, which lands in the chapter’s average tier (10% to 20%). The result is a percent, so 15.0 means 15%. Income and spending need to cover the same period; a monthly spending total against a yearly salary gives a rate that is badly wrong.


What do the benchmark tiers look like in dollars?
The chapter gives four benchmarks: under 10% is the danger zone, 10% to 20% is average, 20% to 30% is strong, and 30% or more is the path to financial independence. Percentages are easy to compare but hard to picture, so the chapter converts one example from each tier into dollars on a $45,000 income:



Annual dollars saved at four savings rate tiers on a $45,000 income


Each bar is income minus spending. Because savings_rate() accepts arrays, one call can work backward from the dollars in each bar to the tier it belongs to:

saved = [3600, 6750, 11250, 15750]
pl.DataFrame({
    "tier": ["danger zone", "average", "strong", "FI path"],
    "saved": saved,
    "rate": savings_rate(income=45000, spending=[45000 - s for s in saved]),
})


shape: (4, 3)tiersavedratestri64f64"danger zone"36008.0"average"675015.0"strong"1125025.0"FI path"1575035.0


The rates come back as 8, 15, 25, and 35, one for each bar. Moving from the danger zone to the strong tier on the same salary means saving an extra $7,650 a year.


Variations
The chapter’s central claim is that savings rate matters more than income. It compares someone earning $45,000 and spending $36,000 with someone earning $75,000 and spending $67,500. Passing both people to savings_rate() at once gives their rates:

earners = pl.DataFrame({
    "income": [45000, 75000],
    "spending": [36000, 67500],
})
earners = earners.with_columns(
    saved=pl.col("income") - pl.col("spending"),
    rate=savings_rate(income=earners["income"], spending=earners["spending"]),
)
earners


shape: (2, 4)incomespendingsavedratei64i64i64f644500036000900020.07500067500750010.0


The lower earner saves 20% and the higher earner saves 10%. To see where each one ends up, we can borrow future_value_series() from Investing Basics. It grows a yearly contribution at 7% (rate is a decimal per period, and here the period is a year):

years = [23, 24, 25, 26]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "saves_20_pct": future_value_series(contribution=9000, rate=0.07, periods=years),
    "saves_10_pct": future_value_series(contribution=7500, rate=0.07, periods=years),
})


shape: (4, 3)yearssaves_20_pctsaves_10_pcti64f64f6423480925.268097400771.05674824523590.036864436325.0307225569241.339444474367.7828726618088.233205515073.527671


The $45,000 earner crosses $500,000 in year 24, and the $75,000 earner crosses it in year 26. That matches the chapter’s chart. The higher saver also lives on $36,000 a year, so they need a smaller pile to stop working.






WarningLimits



savings_rate() does one subtraction and one division, so it leaves a few things to you:

It doesn’t know which income you mean. The chapter uses take home pay here, while Automating Savings measures the rate on gross pay because 401(k) contributions come out before taxes. The same paycheck gives a different rate on each base.
It doesn’t check that income and spending cover the same period.
It returns a negative rate when spending exceeds income instead of raising an error.
It raises an error when income is zero or negative:


savings_rate(income=0, spending=500)

     12 
     13     From the [Savings Strategies](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/fm-finance/savings_strategies.html)
   (...)     40     15.0

---> 38     raise ValueError(f"`{arg}` must be greater than 0.")
     39 return out

ValueError: `income` must be greater than 0.







Putting it together
Back to the first job saving $480 a month. The chapter says savings should be protected before they grow, so the first stop is an emergency fund. The Emergency Fund chapter uses $2,400 a month in essential expenses and a four month target. emergency_fund_target() sets the goal, and months_to_ef_goal() counts the months to reach it at $480 a month:

monthly_saved = 3200 - 2720
ef_target = emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=2400, months=4)
ef_months = months_to_ef_goal(
    target=ef_target, current_balance=0, monthly_contribution=monthly_saved
)
ef_target, ef_months

(9600.0, 20)


At a 15% savings rate, the $9,600 fund is full in 20 months. After that, the same $480 can go to investing instead. future_value_series() takes a monthly rate here, so the 7% yearly return is divided by 12:

invested = future_value_series(contribution=monthly_saved, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12)
invested

585586.0779724534


Thirty years of $480 a month could grow to about $585,586. Nothing about the salary changed; the savings rate did all the work.


Recap
Your savings rate is the lever you fully control, and savings_rate() measures it as a percent of income. One call can check a single paycheck, place several savings amounts on the chapter’s benchmark tiers, or compare people with different salaries. Paired with the emergency fund and investing functions, it shows how a modest rate turns into a protected cushion and then long term wealth.

title: Estate Planning
text:
Your estate is everything you own and everything you owe. Estate planning math asks two things about it: what is it worth, and how much of it do your beneficiary forms control? In this page I’ll answer both with net_worth() and beneficiary_share(), using the 25 year old from the Estate Planning chapter of the book so you can check each result.

The estate functions
Both functions take a dict of name to amount, as the book does. A plain list of amounts works too.








Function
Returns
Units




net_worth()
total assets minus total debts
dollars (a float)


beneficiary_share()
the share of assets with a named beneficiary
a decimal (0.8875 is 88.75%)





What is your estate worth?
The chapter’s example is a 25 year old with a 401(k), a Roth IRA, some savings, and a car. On the other side are a car loan and a small credit card balance. The bar model puts what you own on one bar and what you owe on the other:



Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old


Net worth is the length of the top bar minus the length of the bottom bar. net_worth() adds up each dict and subtracts:

assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
debts = {"car_loan": 6000, "credit_card": 1000}
worth = net_worth(assets, debts)
worth

28000.0


The estate is worth $28,000: $35,000 in assets minus $7,000 in debts.


How much do your beneficiary forms control?
Now add life insurance through work. Many employers give free coverage equal to one year of salary, say $45,000. It isn’t part of net worth while you’re alive, but it pays out when you die. The bar below shows everything that would pass to someone else, split by what decides who gets it:



What decides who gets each part of the estate


The green sections are decided by forms you fill out online; only the vermillion section depends on a will. beneficiary_share() divides the green sections by the whole bar:

with_beneficiary = {
    "401k": 12000,
    "roth_ira": 6000,
    "life_insurance": 45000,
    "savings_pod": 8000,
}
without_beneficiary = {"car": 9000}
share = beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary)
share

0.8875


About 89% of the estate is decided by forms that take minutes to fill out. That’s why the book puts beneficiary designations ahead of a will for most young people. Note that the result is a decimal, not a percent.


Variations
beneficiary_share() takes one estate at a time, so a list comprehension compares several. Here is the same estate with fewer forms filed:

scenarios = {
    "all forms filed": (with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary),
    "no POD on savings": (
        {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000},
        {"savings": 8000, "car": 9000},
    ),
    "retirement forms only": (
        {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000},
        {"life_insurance": 45000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000},
    ),
}
pl.DataFrame({
    "scenario": list(scenarios),
    "share": [beneficiary_share(w, wo) for w, wo in scenarios.values()],
})


shape: (3, 2)scenariosharestrf64"all forms filed"0.8875"no POD on savings"0.7875"retirement forms only"0.225


Skipping the life insurance form costs the most, because it is the largest item. (Most employer life insurance asks for a beneficiary at enrollment; the last row shows what happens if you leave it blank.)






WarningLimits



net_worth() adds the values you give it. It doesn’t know what a car is worth next year, so use today’s market value, and enter debts as positive balances. It ignores taxes owed on retirement accounts and the costs of probate.
beneficiary_share() returns a decimal, unlike the ratio functions that return percents. It ignores joint ownership, which also passes outside a will, and it stops with a ValueError when total assets aren’t greater than 0:

beneficiary_share({}, {"car": 0})


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[5], line 1
----> 1 beneficiary_share({}, {"car": 0})

File ~/projects/pkgs/Python/perfinpy/src/perfinpy/estate_planning.py:97, in beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary)
     95 total = named + _total(without_beneficiary, "without_beneficiary")
     96 if total <= 0:
---> 97     raise ValueError("Total assets must be greater than 0.")
     98 return named / total

ValueError: Total assets must be greater than 0.



Both functions raise a TypeError for text and a ValueError for missing values.




Putting it together
Estates change as you save. Five years from now, suppose the retirement accounts grow at 7% a year (with future_value() from Investing Basics), savings reach $15,000, the car is paid off and worth $6,000, and the credit card is cleared:

retirement = future_value(present_value=[12000, 6000], rate=0.07, years=5)
assets_later = {
    "401k": retirement[0],
    "roth_ira": retirement[1],
    "savings": 15000,
    "car": 6000,
}
worth_later = net_worth(assets_later, debts={"car_loan": 0, "credit_card": 0})
share_later = beneficiary_share(
    {
        "401k": retirement[0],
        "roth_ira": retirement[1],
        "life_insurance": 45000,
        "savings_pod": 15000,
    },
    {"car": 6000},
)
round(worth_later, 2), round(share_later, 4)

(46245.93, 0.9342)


Net worth grows to $46,246, and the forms now decide 93% of the estate. The bigger the accounts get, the more those ten minute forms matter.


Recap
net_worth() gives the starting number for any estate plan: what you own minus what you owe. beneficiary_share() shows how much of that estate passes by beneficiary forms instead of a will. For most young people the answer is most of it, so fill in those forms first.
This is the last chapter of the book and the last page of the guide.

title: Income
text:
A bigger paycheck only builds wealth if some of it stays put. The book’s Income chapter turns that idea into three questions. How much does steady saving grow into? How much of each paycheck is committed before you spend a dollar? And what is a raise worth if you invest part of it? In this page I’ll answer each one with perfinpy, using the same numbers as the chapter.








Function
Returns
Units




wealth_formula()
the balance after saving part of a yearly income every year
dollars; rates go in as decimals


fixed_cost_ratio()
monthly fixed costs as a share of take home pay
percent (55, not 0.55)


raise_invested_value()
the balance after investing part of a monthly raise every month
dollars; rates go in as decimals



The units follow the package conventions described in Get started: rates go in as decimals and ratios come out as percents.

How much does steady saving grow into?
The chapter builds on Scott Galloway’s wealth formula (focus plus stoicism, time, and diversification multiplied together). To put numbers on it, the book uses a worker who earns about the 2025 median for full time workers. This worker saves a fixed share of income every year and invests it. The scenario below sets those inputs:

income = 62400
save_pct = 0.15
annual_return = 0.08
wealth_years = 40

This worker earns $62,400 a year and saves 15% of it, which comes to $9,360 a year. Those savings earn 8% a year for 40 years. Each bar below is the balance at a checkpoint, split into the money put in and what it grew into.



Money put in vs. growth at each checkpoint


The green layer rises in a straight line because it is one deposit per year. The blue layer is every deposit growing for the years it has left, and it is the part that takes over. wealth_formula() adds up all of those growing deposits in one call:

wealth_40 = wealth_formula(
    median_income=income,
    savings_rate=save_pct,
    annual_return=annual_return,
    years=wealth_years,
)
wealth_40

2424769.0151255885


After 40 years the balance is about $2,424,769. Only $374,400 of that is money the worker put in; the other $2,050,369 is growth.


How much of your paycheck is already spoken for?
Fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, utilities) are the bills you can’t easily change from one month to the next. The book’s example is a first job with these monthly numbers:

fixed_costs = 1760
take_home = 3200
ceiling_pct = 60

This paycheck brings in $3,200 of take home pay a month, and $1,760 of it goes to fixed costs. The book suggests keeping fixed costs under 60% of take home pay, which is $1,920 here. The bar below cuts the paycheck into ten equal pieces and marks that ceiling.



Take home pay split into fixed costs and flexible spending


fixed_cost_ratio() divides the fixed costs by take home pay and returns a percent:

ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs=fixed_costs, take_home=take_home)
ratio

55.00000000000001


Fixed costs take 55% of this paycheck, under the 60% ceiling. That leaves $160 of room before a new commitment pushes the budget past it. The Budgeting page picks up from here and splits the flexible part of the paycheck.


What is a raise really worth?
The chapter recommends splitting every raise: half goes to your lifestyle and half gets invested. The book’s raise adds a fixed amount to monthly take home pay:

monthly_raise = 400
share = 0.5
raise_rate = 0.07
raise_years = 25

A raise of $400 a month split in half sends $200 a month into investments. That money earns 7% a year for 25 years. The bars below show the balance at each checkpoint.



A monthly raise contribution invested at each checkpoint


raise_invested_value() takes the whole raise and the share you invest, then compounds the contributions monthly:

raise_value = raise_invested_value(
    monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
    invest_share=share,
    rate=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
raise_value

162014.33860462217


Half of the raise grows to about $162,014. The contributions add up to $60,000, so growth adds about $102,014. The Investing Basics page returns to this future value of contributions formula with future_value_series().


Variations
Both growth functions accept arrays, so we can compare options in one call. The savings rate is the stoicism lever in Galloway’s formula. The code below keeps the income, return, and horizon from the first section and changes only the share saved:

rates = [0.10, 0.15, 0.20]
pl.DataFrame({
    "savings_rate": rates,
    "yearly_savings": [income * r for r in rates],
    "wealth": wealth_formula(
        median_income=income,
        savings_rate=rates,
        annual_return=annual_return,
        years=wealth_years,
    ),
})


shape: (3, 3)savings_rateyearly_savingswealthf64f64f640.16240.01.6165e60.159360.02.4248e60.212480.03.2330e6


The same idea works for the raise. Here is the $400 raise with a quarter, half, three quarters, and all of it invested:

shares = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0]
pl.DataFrame({
    "invest_share": shares,
    "per_month": [monthly_raise * s for s in shares],
    "value": raise_invested_value(
        monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
        invest_share=shares,
        rate=raise_rate,
        years=raise_years,
    ),
})


shape: (4, 3)invest_shareper_monthvaluef64f64f640.25100.081007.1693020.5200.0162014.3386050.75300.0243021.5079071.0400.0324028.677209


Both tables scale in a straight line with the share saved because the return and horizon don’t change. The horizon is where the curve bends, as the bar models above show.






WarningLimits




wealth_formula() assumes one deposit at the end of every year, the same income every year (no raises), and the same return every year. It ignores taxes, fees, and inflation, so results are in future dollars.
raise_invested_value() makes the same assumptions with a deposit at the end of every month and monthly compounding.
A 0% return in either function gives the plain sum of the deposits instead of nan.
fixed_cost_ratio() raises a ValueError when take_home is 0 or negative. It doesn’t decide which bills count as fixed, and the 60% ceiling is a guideline from the book, not an argument.
The growth functions reject text and nan but not negative values, so check the signs of your inputs.





Putting it together
The worker from the fixed cost section gets the $400 raise. Investing half is the easy part; the real question is where the lifestyle half goes. If it stays flexible (dinners, trips), fixed costs don’t change. If it goes to a pricier apartment, fixed costs rise by the full lifestyle half. The code below compares the fixed cost ratio before the raise and under both choices:

new_take_home = take_home + monthly_raise
plans = pl.DataFrame({
    "plan": [
        "before the raise",
        "lifestyle half stays flexible",
        "lifestyle half goes to rent",
    ],
    "fixed_costs": [
        float(fixed_costs),
        float(fixed_costs),
        fixed_costs + monthly_raise * (1 - share),
    ],
    "take_home": [take_home, new_take_home, new_take_home],
})
plans = plans.with_columns(
    ratio=fixed_cost_ratio(
        fixed_costs=plans["fixed_costs"].to_numpy(),
        take_home=plans["take_home"].to_numpy(),
    )
)
plans


shape: (3, 4)planfixed_coststake_homeratiostrf64i64f64"before the raise"1760.0320055.0"lifestyle half stays flexible"1760.0360048.888889"lifestyle half goes to rent"1960.0360054.444444


Keeping the lifestyle half flexible drops the ratio to 48.9%. Moving it into rent leaves the ratio at 54.4%, almost where it started, so the raise buys very little breathing room. This is the lifestyle inflation the chapter warns about: the upgrade becomes a permanent bill.
The invested half grows the same way in both plans. The code below values it twice: once with monthly deposits, and once with a single deposit at the end of each year. The yearly version uses wealth_formula(), whose median_income argument accepts any yearly amount:

monthly_value = raise_invested_value(
    monthly_raise=monthly_raise,
    invest_share=share,
    rate=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
yearly_value = wealth_formula(
    median_income=monthly_raise * 12,
    savings_rate=share,
    annual_return=raise_rate,
    years=raise_years,
)
monthly_value, yearly_value

(162014.33860462217, 151797.69051849932)


The same dollars come out about $10,217 ahead when they’re invested every month. Each monthly deposit starts growing sooner, which is one more reason to automate the transfer the day the raise arrives.


Recap
wealth_formula() and raise_invested_value() show how a steady deposit turns into a balance that is mostly growth. Time does more of the work than the deposits do. fixed_cost_ratio() tells you how much of each paycheck is committed before you spend anything, and returns a percent you can compare against the 60% ceiling. Together they make the chapter’s advice measurable: keep fixed costs low, and invest part of every raise before your lifestyle absorbs it.

Income in Personal Finance: a field manual
Reference: wealth_formula(), fixed_cost_ratio(), raise_invested_value()

title: Investing Basics
text: Investing math is mostly one idea (compounding) applied a few different ways. You want to know what money invested today grows into, how long it takes to double, and what a monthly habit adds up to. You also want to know how much of a return is left once inflation takes its share. In this page I’ll answer those questions with future_value(), rule_of_72(), future_value_series(), and real_return(). The numbers come from the Investing Basics chapter of the book, so you can check every result against it.

title: Investing Basics
text:
How long until money doubles?
The rule of 72 is a shortcut: divide 72 by the yearly return (as a percent) to estimate the years it takes to double. rule_of_72() is the one function in the package that takes a percent, so 7% goes in as 7:

double_years = rule_of_72(annual_return_pct=7)
double_years

10.285714285714286


At 7%, money doubles about every 10.3 years. That matches the bar model: $10,000 at year 0 is close to $20,000 at year 10 and close to $40,000 at year 20.

title: Investing Basics
text:
One call compares every checkpoint
Passing several horizons to periods reproduces each bar in the contributions bar model, with the money contributed alongside:

years = [10, 20, 30]
pl.DataFrame({
    "years": years,
    "contributed": [500 * 12 * y for y in years],
    "value": future_value_series(
        contribution=500, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=[y * 12 for y in years]
    ),
})


shape: (3, 3)yearscontributedvaluei64i64f64106000086542.40371720120000260463.32991330180000609985.497888








WarningLimits



These functions are for planning, not prediction. A few things they don’t do:

future_value() and future_value_series() assume the same return every year. Real returns bounce around, and they ignore taxes, fund fees, and inflation unless you pass a real return.
future_value_series() assumes each contribution is made at the end of the period. The rate is per period, so passing a yearly rate with monthly periods gives a much larger (wrong) answer. A 0% rate returns the sum of the contributions.
rule_of_72() is an estimate, and it takes a percent (7, not 0.07). A return of 0 or less raises a ValueError, because money that doesn’t grow never doubles.
real_return() returns a decimal, not a percent.

title: apply_rules()
text:
Categorize transactions with keyword rules.


Usage
Source


apply_rules(df, rules)


Each row of rules holds a regular expression (Pattern) and the Category it assigns. Rules are tried in order and the first match wins; matching ignores case. Descriptions that match no rule get "Other". From the Tracking Spending chapter.


Parameters


df: pl.DataFrame

Transactions with a string Description column.

rules: pl.DataFrame

Rules with string Pattern and Category columns.





Returns


 polars.DataFrame

df with a Category column added (or replaced).





Raises


 TypeError

If df or rules is not a polars DataFrame.

 ValueError

If a required column is missing.





Examples
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from perfinpy import apply_rules
>>> transactions = pl.DataFrame(
...     {"Description": ["SAFEWAY #123", "NETFLIX.COM", "ATM FEE"]}
... )
>>> rules = pl.DataFrame(
...     {"Pattern": ["safeway", "netflix"],
...      "Category": ["Groceries", "Subscriptions"]}
... )
>>> apply_rules(transactions, rules)["Category"].to_list()
[‘Groceries’, ‘Subscriptions’, ‘Other’]

title: idr_monthly_payment()
text:
Income driven repayment (IDR) monthly payment.


Usage
Source


idr_monthly_payment(
    agi, poverty_guideline=15960, threshold_pct=1.5, payment_rate=0.1
)


Discretionary income is adjusted gross income (AGI) above threshold_pct times the poverty guideline. The yearly payment is payment_rate of that, split into 12 months and rounded to cents. From the Managing Debt chapter.


Parameters


agi: ArrayLike

Adjusted gross income.

poverty_guideline: ArrayLike = 15960

Federal poverty guideline for the household size. Defaults to 15960 (one person).

threshold_pct: ArrayLike = 1.5

Multiple of the poverty guideline that is protected. Defaults to 1.5 (150%).

payment_rate: ArrayLike = 0.1

Share of discretionary income paid each year. Defaults to 0.10.





Returns


 float or numpy.ndarray

Monthly payments.





Raises


 TypeError

If an argument is not numeric.

 ValueError

If an argument contains missing values.





Examples
>>> from perfinpy import idr_monthly_payment
>>> # IBR: $50,000 AGI, 150% threshold, 10% rate
>>> idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000)
217.17
>>> # IBR for loans before July 2014: 15% rate
>>> idr_monthly_payment(agi=50000, payment_rate=0.15)
325.75
